jobs.title: Research Engineer, AI Monitoring
jobs.description: About Anthropic Anthropic’s mission is to create reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems. We want AI to be safe and beneficial for our users and for society as a whole. Our team is a quickly growing group of committed researchers, engineers, policy experts, and business leaders working together to build beneficial AI systems. About the role Our team builds, tests, deploys, and monitors the classifiers that block internal agents from taking dangerous actions. These classifiers run across RL, evals, and internal deployments, and are designed to catch things like sandbox escape attempts or exfiltration of sensitive data. When a classifier flags an action, it can block the action before the tool call runs, end the task, and alert a human . This is one layer of a defence-in-depth with several layers that reinforce each other: what our classifiers flag feeds into offline monitoring, and the findings from that go back into better classifiers and safer environment design. The work combines research and production engineering: The research problem is building high recall and high precision classifiers to catch rare, novel, and sometimes adversarial behaviour. There are also several narrow research questions to answer - for example, how to deploy safety classifiers inside training environments without incentivising models to evade them. Some research also builds on the multi-stage designs described in our work on Claude Code auto mode and Constitutional Classifiers . The engineering problem is shipping these classifiers into the critical path of research and product work. These classifiers need to cover a huge volume of traffic while operating within cost, latency and availability constraints. Day to day, much of our work is done with Claude: you ll direct agents to run experiments and ship code, and review what they produce. jobs.title: Embedded Software Engineer - N3XT (m/f/d)
jobs.description: The Embedded Engineer brings N3XT’s hardware to life. You write firmware for sensor front-ends, payload controllers, power systems and communication modules, bring up new boards with the hardware engineers, and build the low-level interfaces the application software depends on. Prototypes in N3XT move fast. A board designed a few weeks ago lands on your bench, runs your firmware the same day and is on the test field by the end of the week. You sit between hardware and software and keep both sides honest about timing, power and interfaces. What is your Day to Day Mission: Develop firmware in C and C++ for microcontrollers and SoCs (e.g. STM32, NXP i.MX , Xilinx Zynq), bare-metal or on an RTOS. Bring up new boards together with the hardware engineers: drivers, peripherals, debugging with JTAG, oscilloscope and logic analyser. Implement communication interfaces and protocols: CAN, UART, SPI, I²C, Ethernet, USB and radio links. Integrate embedded Linux on compute modules: bootloader, kernel configuration, device tree and drivers. Write real-time firmware for sensor acquisition and control, with attention to timing, power and reliability. Define and document the interfaces to the application software and to the autopilot. Support field tests and diagnose problems directly on the hardware. Document firmware and interfaces for handover to line engineering. What you bring to the team: Degree in electrical engineering, computer engineering, mechatronics or a related field. At least three years of embedded software development on systems that shipped or were used in the field. Experience in at least one of our domains: Air, Land, Sea or Software. Strong C and C++ for resource-constrained systems; experience with an RTOS such as FreeRTOS or Zephyr. Hands-on board bring-up and hardware debugging; fluent reading of schematics and datasheets. jobs.description: Summary of the Role: Maze is a well-funded Series A startup using AI agents to fix vulnerability management for enterprise security teams. Our research team finds things worth talking about every week: how real vulnerabilities get exploited, which ones matter, and why most of the noise doesn't.
